transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I suppose the main reason I came in is that I’ve started noticing—or maybe other people have helped me notice—that I’m forever getting up when I’m supposed to be sitting still. It sounds small when I say it like that, but it happens in meetings at school, or even at dinner with friends or family. Everyone else is seated, and I’ll suddenly be on my feet, saying I need to refill my coffee, or check a handout, or go to the back of the room for something.

And the thing is, when I think about it afterward, it’s not usually urgent. Sometimes there isn’t really a good reason at all. I just feel like I need to move, or I’m up before I’ve properly thought it through. As a teacher I can sort of disguise it a bit, because moving around the room can look purposeful, but in meetings it’s more obvious. I’ve become a bit embarrassed by it, especially when I realize I’m the only one who can’t seem to just stay seated like everyone else.
Do you often feel restless or have an urge to move even when you’re not trying to accomplish something specific?

Yes, I do. It’s not always that I’m trying to get something done, exactly, though I usually find a reason for it afterward. Since the house got quieter—my youngest left for college—it’s become more noticeable to me. I’ll tell myself, “Tonight I’m going to sit down, maybe read, maybe just rest,” and then somehow I’m moving from lesson planning to putting in a load of laundry, then remembering something for softball practice, then chopping vegetables for some community event I said I’d help with.

And none of it is necessarily frantic, if that makes sense. It’s more like I don’t naturally come to a stop. Even when there’s no emergency, I’m up and doing the next thing, and then the next thing. Sometimes I think the quiet makes it worse, because without the children in and out of the house, I notice my own restlessness more. I can promise myself a calm evening and still find I’ve barely sat down.
Do you find it hard to focus or stay attentive, especially during tasks that require sustained mental effort, like reading, planning lessons, or even watching a movie?

I’m not sure I’d say that’s the main thing I’ve noticed, honestly. I mean, everyone loses the thread now and then, don’t they? Especially teaching all day and then coming home with a pile of things still running through your head.

With reading or lesson planning, I can usually manage if I’m interested or if there’s a deadline. I might get up to make tea or sharpen a pencil or move papers around, but I don’t know that I’d call it a focus problem exactly. It’s more that I don’t always stay physically settled while I’m doing it.

Watching a movie… well, I suppose I don’t always sit perfectly still through one, but I haven’t really thought of it as not paying attention. If someone asked me to describe whether I have trouble sustaining attention, I’d have to think about that more. It hasn’t stood out to me in the same way as the needing to move around.
Do you find yourself talking more than you intend to, interrupting others during conversations, or acting on impulse without thinking things through?

Yes… yes, I do, especially the interrupting part. I’m a little embarrassed to admit that, because I don’t mean to be rude, but in group conversations I’ll often jump in before the other person has properly finished.

It happens at book club quite a bit, actually. Someone will be explaining what they thought about a chapter, and halfway through I can feel my answer sort of forming in my head, and then it just comes out. I’ll realize a second later that they hadn’t finished their point. And it’s the same in curriculum meetings at school. Someone is laying out an idea or a concern, and I already think I know where they’re going, or I have a response ready, and I blurt it out before I’ve really stopped myself.

I usually notice afterward from the look on their face, or when they go quiet, and then I feel awful and try to say, “Sorry, go on.” It isn’t that I don’t care what they’re saying. It’s more like the thought arrives so fast that if I don’t say it right then, it feels like I’ll lose it, and then suddenly I’ve cut across them.
Looking back, were you someone who had trouble staying still or tended to act impulsively before you were 12 years old, such as in grade school?

Yes, looking back, I think I was like that even quite young. I didn’t think of it as anything serious at the time, of course—it was just “how I was”—but my report cards used to say things like I was bright, or capable, but that I had trouble staying in my seat or waiting my turn.

My mother used to joke about it, actually. She’d say I wore a little path between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was even ten, because I was always getting up for some reason. I can still picture those old classrooms, and me finding excuses to move around. It wasn’t that I was trying to be difficult, at least I don’t remember feeling that way. I just didn’t seem to stay put very well. And the waiting-my-turn comments came up too, I think—like I’d know the answer and want to say it right then.
